morning.title: Pakistan extends airspace ban on Indian aircraft until November 24
morning.text:
Pakistan has extended its airspace ban on Indian-registered aircraft and planes owned, operated or leased by Indian airlines for another month, until November 24, according to the country’s airports authority.
The restriction, initially imposed on April 23, 2025, has been extended periodically since then amid strained relations between the two neighbouring countries.
The Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA) announced the extension in a post on X on Saturday, saying the restriction also covers military flights.
The latest extension will remain in effect until 4:59 am (local time) on November 24, 2026, according to the authority.
A PAA spokesperson said a fresh Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) had been issued to extend the ban, Geo News reported.
Pakistan’s airspace is divided into two flight information regions (FIRs) — Karachi and Lahore, according to a Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority (PCAA) document from 2022. The latest NOTAM applies to both the Karachi and Lahore FIRs.
India and Pakistan imposed reciprocal airspace restrictions on each other’s aircraft following the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack in the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.
India accused Pakistan of involvement in the attack, an allegation Islamabad denied. The incident was followed by a sharp escalation in diplomatic and military tensions between the two countries.
India closed its airspace to Pakistani airlines on April 30, 2025, in response to Pakistan’s move.
Pakistan has imposed airspace restrictions on Indian aircraft during previous periods of heightened tensions, including the 1999 Kargil conflict and the 2019 Pulwama crisis, according to Geo News.
The continuing airspace restrictions have affected airline operations between the two countries, forcing carriers to take longer routes on some international flights.

morning.title: IAF Seeks 150 Trainer Jets: Will Private Companies Finally Take on HAL?
morning.text:
The Indian Air Force’s (IAF) decision to procure around 150 new Stage-III jet trainers to replace its ageing Hawk Mk-132 fleet offers India an unique opportunity to do something truly remarkable. The government must now strongly consider incentivizing the Indian private sector to develop an Advanced Jet Trainer and compete against HAL, rather than allow the requirement to languish as yet another “domestic” programme for one company.
IAF issued an RFI for around 150 Stage-III (F) trainer aircraft in August 2026, with responses due on October 5. The new planes would comprise the final step in pilot training before transitioning to front-line fighters. A requirement of 150 aircraft is significant enough to warrant bidders’ utmost attention in terms of investments.
The new jet trainer would prepare Indian Air Force pilots for the next generation of combat aircraft, including Tejas, Rafale, and AMCA, and expose them to cutting-edge technologies like radar, electronic warfare, and network-centric warfare. HAL has considerable experience with the Hawk Mk-132 and has developed indigenous trainer aircraft like HLFT-42 and Tejas Sports .
However, requiring a private Indian company or consortium to develop an alternative AJT would generate healthy competition. The government could also issue a separate parallel development proposal for the AJT to private bidders, giving them access to testing infrastructure, certification support, and potentially some government-owned technologies, while mitigating the risk by sharing the development costs.
The new jet trainer should not be viewed only as an evolution over the current trainers. The RFI highlights that the new trainer would be significantly more advanced than the current ones, incorporating a glass cockpit, HOTAS, FADEC, and a software-defined radio, with options for future expansion and growth.
While the RFI indicates that the new trainer will use an existing powerplant, the most challenging aspect of the request is that it proposes building a clean-sheet jet. Such an undertaking would be prohibitively expensive and technically challenging for any private company, thus deterring potential bidders. The government needs to assure private companies that it will purchase the planes if they can satisfy the IAF’s requirements and obtain the necessary certifications.
The 150-plane order has enough potential to become a reality if the government can convince a private company that there will be an assured market for its product. To achieve that, the government could guarantee purchases of successfully developed indigenous aircraft for the IAF and the other services, subject to their meeting the required specifications and certifications.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

morning.title: The UN Loses Credibility Due to Arbitrary, Unverified Reports: India
morning.text:
Arbitrary reports based on unverifiable hearsay have led to the UN losing its credibility, India has warned while rejecting “outright” a report by the monitor for freedom of peaceful assembly.
“A sweeping charge against the world’s largest youth population, resting on anonymous and unverified claims is not evidence”, Indian diplomat Anuj Swarup said on Friday, taking exception to the Special Rapporteur’s report on the Rights to Freedom of Peaceful Assembly and of Association.
“This level of arbitrary report writing is precisely the reason that the United Nations and its institutions have lost credibility”, he said at a meeting in New York of the General Assembly’s Third Committee that deals with social and humanitarian issues.
“It is hearsay dressed up as a UN report, and my delegation rejects it outright”, he said.
The report by Special Rapporteur Gina Romero said, “Young people from India reported retaliation or stigmatisation for discussing mental health or gender justice”.
The footnote to the claim in the report attributed it to a “submission” without further identifying the source.
“A mandate holder who relies on anonymous inputs to generalise for 1.4 billion people does a disservice to the very mandate she holds”, said Swarup, a first secretary in India’s UN mission in Geneva.
This was the second time this week that India issued a warning about the UN human rights mechanism losing its credibility through arbitrary reports.
Swarup on Wednesday said Human Rights Commissioner Volker Turk was following double standards in how he reports on violent responses to protests.
“Violent responses to protests in our neighbourhood, as well as in the West, have gone uncommented” in the reports Turk, he said.
“Such double standards contribute to loss of trust” in the high commissioner, he said.
While criticising the special rapporteur’s submission on Friday, Swarup said, “Ironically, the same report notes that young Indians created a satirical political movement”.
“In which repressive state does a satirical youth party question the government, marches on the capital and then sits across the table with senior national leaders?”, he asked rhetorically, referring to the Cockroach Janta Party.
He said Romero probably missed Turk’s statement “in the Human Rights Council last month that dialogue with young leaders is far more effective in the context of youth-led movement in India”.
Turk said on September 7, “The recent protests in India showed the best response is dialogue with youth leaders, not the excessive use of force”.
“The true testament of democracy in action” is how India handled the youth protests against examination irregularities, he said.
“When students protested this summer over irregularities in public examinations, the government engaged constructively with the youth” and “within weeks, Parliament amended the Public Examinations Act”, he said.
It doubled punishments for paper leaks, carried out a systemic examination overhaul and created fast-track courts in every state specifically dedicated to prosecuting individuals involved in exam fraud, he said.
Responding to Swarup’s criticism, Romero acknowledged, “India is the biggest democracy in the world” and “they have several participatory bodies and scenarios to include the voices of youths”.
“But also, we have youths in the streets protesting”, she said, repeating her criticism.
Romero, a Colombian activist, was appointed rapporteur by the Human Rights Council.
Rapporteurs are not UN staffers and serve in their personal capacities without a salary.
(IANS)

morning.title: Chinese Netizens Mock India’s Arms Exports and Reliability
morning.text:
A number of Chinese social media discussions have appeared regarding the alleged reliability and indigenization of Indian-made equipment, stating that it would be more appropriate to rely on equipment which demonstrated its combat performance, rather than being selected on a political or budgetary basis.
The Chinese discussions compared Indian military equipment to that of other nations through the lens of a military game, suggesting that the former may demonstrate better performance in a simulated environment than in actual combat. The posts also state that the game does not account for reliability or technical failures, while one of the comments suggested that it would be unreasonable to purchase Indian equipment over other foreign alternatives.
One of the arguments made in the comments was that equipment reliability and performance during operations was a more relevant metric than specifications, including those demonstrated in a military game. The posts also suggested that India’s ability to provide spares and maintenance was questionable, while several of the comments suggested assessing the ability of India to provide reliable equipment. While the comments touch upon valid points concerning the procurement process, the reliability of Indian equipment is not an open and evident fact, as the criticism also demonstrates.
Procurement decisions should rely on evidence which demonstrates the level of performance, maintenance and availability, technical support throughout the lifespan of the equipment, as well as the cost-benefit ratio. A single assessment which regards an entire nation’s defence industry as unreliable does not account for the nuances of the defence production process.
One of the points made in the comments regarded India’s position in the global defence market, with one of the posts suggesting that it was analogous to China during the Cold War. As such, the comment suggested that the only reason why India was able to sell its equipment was because it was similar to Russian designs or was a cheaper alternative.
The assertion is demonstrably false, as India possesses a diverse defence industry which utilises both foreign and domestic components for its products, with some systems being built domestically, while others being produced abroad under India’s licence. The degree to which individual platforms are indigenous varies greatly, as does the degree to which they rely on foreign components.
Additionally, India’s domestic defence industry has had issues concerning the reliability and support of its products, while its foreign sales were historically low due to limited support and reliability. Contemporary India does not possess the same limitations in terms of production, while several systems which rely on India’s domestic development and design capabilities are produced by its domestic companies, as well as several foreign manufacturers. The narrative which suggests that Indian equipment is exclusively copies of foreign designs is demonstrably incorrect, as are the claims which suggest that Indian equipment is completely domestic.
The most reasonable point made by the Chinese social media posts regarded India’s role in the international defence market and its ability to sell its equipment abroad. The comment suggested that equipment purchases should be based on combat performance, rather than supporting one’s geopolitical goals.
While it is evident that defence procurements are usually based on a variety of criteria, including combat performance, cost, rate of deliveries, technology transfers, domestic production rates, political alliance, the presence of sanctions, and the ability to acquire spares and receive support, the comment’s points are valid. India’s foreign sales would be enhanced not by attempting to replace the purchases of its foreign competitors, but by providing the guarantee of quality, performance, and continued support after-sales.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

IAF Chief Manned Unmanned Teaming Vision Makes Real-Time Drone Classification India’s Next Air Defence Frontier
morning.text:
Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh has laid out the future of Indian air power with a very clear message: the battlespace of the future will be one of manned aircraft and drones operating together in the same airspace at the same time. It will not be one or the other. He made this point at a Society of Indian Defence Manufacturers workshop in New Delhi on 30th July 2026. The future will be a mix of manned fighters, long range vectors and a full spectrum of unmanned systems (from micro drones to aircraft sized UAS) all operating in the same volume of air. Seamless integration of all of these systems will be a pre-requisite for any operation.
This was the doctrinal framework he set out in his May address to the Centre for Aerospace Power and Strategic Studies where he described the evolution of the drone from being ‘eyes in the sky’ to being ‘claws in the sky’ and stated that the future is indeed manned and unmanned teaming.
The Air Chief’s most cogent warning was about fratricide. He made it quite clear to the SIDM that the IAF must ensure that no friendly UAV is inadvertently engaged. He also indicated that talks are already underway with the MoCA on a mechanism to differentiate between legitimate and rogue drones. The issue he was highlighting was not detection per se. India’s counter-UAS grid has been proven in action during Operation Sindoor in May 2025 when it successfully neutralised a swarm of incoming drones using a layered approach. The real issue is classification at range and at speed. You have to be able to tell the difference between a friendly and a hostile asset before you make a decision, with a manned platform in the same airspace.
This is fundamentally a data fusion problem rather than a single sensor problem. A radar return by itself is not going to tell you whether you have a drone or a bird (they have similar cross sections at range) and in the presence of significant clutter from buildings and terrain a small UAV can be completely swallowed. An RF sensor by itself will miss anything that isn’t actively transmitting (e.g. a pre-programmed loitering munition flying an autonomous waypoint with no command link). India’s indigenous CUAS architecture (the DRDO D4 system, Bharat Electronics Akashteer integrated air defence control system and Zen Technologies integrated CUAS platform) utilises AI enabled fusion engines to fuse the radar tracks, RF emitter signatures, EO/IR confirmation and acoustic arrays into a single classified object prior to any engagement decision.
The fusion layer takes care of the birds, balloons and weather that would otherwise generate false alarms, classifies the object as a drone and infers the intent from the flight pattern. The result is one track, one classification and one recommended response rather than four separate sensor alarms arriving at an operator under time pressure.
The Indrajaal SkyOS platform (contracted for Navy and Army use in Jan 2026) goes further in this respect by creating a multi-layer engagement log which will correlate radar tracks, RF behaviour, GNSS telemetry patterns and effector command outputs before, during and after an engagement and will assign a unique identifier to each engagement so that the attribution is unambiguous even in the case of multiple counter-drone systems operating in the same area. In the absence of a civil-military UTM framework, a delivery drone and a hostile loitering munition could be indistinguishable to any one sensor.
The Air Chief’s call for a mechanism to be able to tell the difference between a legitimate and a rogue drone is effectively a call for that traffic management layer to be incorporated into the military’s Common Operating Picture so that every legitimate unmanned platform has a distinct signature which the fusion engine can then correlate against known flight plans.
The conversation has now moved from the lab to procurement. The IAF issued two RFI’s in Jan 2026 for counter-swarm systems with AI based threat classification as a key requirement. The SANKALP 2026 seminar revealed plans to fit the IAF’s helicopters with AI based target identification in EO pods, along with micro-missiles and jammers. The HAL Combat Air Teaming System (CATS) programme with the CATS Warrior as the core of the system is the very architecture the Air Chief spoke of, a Tejas variant acting as a mothership to control 2-4 unmanned systems via secure datalinks, with a first flight in 2027.
The key engineering challenge is sensor data compression, taking the input from a range of sensors and reducing it to a set of prioritised cues that can fit within the constraints of the secure datalink so that a single shared picture is available to both the manned cockpit and the unmanned system prior to the action window closing.

morning.title: REUDE Launches India-Made DynoX Thrust Stand for UAV
morning.text:
Indian technology company REUDE Technologies has announced the development of DynoX, an AI-powered propulsion thrust stand designed for UAV and eVTOL propulsion testing. The company claims that the system is designed and made in India and features real-time AI algorithms to detect measurement errors during testing.
REUDE claims that DynoX is capable of providing high-fidelity propulsion test data without requiring conventional post-test data filtering. The platform is designed to cater to propulsion systems ranging from nano-UAV motors to larger aerospace applications. The main claimed advantage of DynoX is the system’s capacity to provide real-time data-processing. REUDE notes that the capability of its AI algorithms to detect and cancel measurement errors in real-time allows for test data to be processed during the test and not require extensive correction after the fact.
The company has not yet revealed detailed information on the AI models, algorithms or validation methodology that enables the claimed error correction capabilities. Independent test data comparing the performance of DynoX to established propulsion test equipment is also not currently available. REUDE notes that DynoX is built with a modular architecture that allows it to be compatible with different motors, ESCs, propellers and sensors. The company claims that this allows the same basic test platform to be adapted to a range of propulsion configurations.
The system makes use of what REUDE describes as space-grade aluminium construction, with the structure being designed around precision measurement requirements.
The company is also highlighting the system’s capacity to act as a plug-and-play system which reduces the setup requirements before propulsion tests can commence. This could be relevant to UAV developers looking to repeatedly evaluate different motor-propeller combinations during the course of aircraft development. REUDE notes that DynoX will be available across seven capacity variants which can cater to propulsion systems ranging from under 1 kg of thrust to over 50 kg.
The smallest variant is identified as RTS Micro which is designed for under 1 kg thrust systems, while the range extends to the RTS Ultra rated for over 50 kg.
This range would allow the platform to address a range of propulsion development requirements, ranging from small motors on nano and micro UAVs to higher-thrust systems for larger unmanned aircraft and eVTOL applications. DynoX is powered by RotriX V3.0, which REUDE describes as an AI-based motor testing platform. The company claims that RotriX provides the underlying testing and data-processing capabilities for propulsion evaluation.

morning.title: Elon Musk Responds to Reliance as Starlink Eyes India Launch
morning.text:
Elon Musk-owned Starlink said it has worked closely with regulators, industry and operators in India for more than 5 years, in a reply to Reliance Industries Ltd (REL) which said that India’s rules apply equally to domestic and foreign companies in the field of satellite communications.
Starlink said it has built a network of dedicated systems, gateways, and other infrastructure all in-country to exclusively serve Indian traffic safely and securely – and all with the requisite government approvals.
“Starlink is ready to connect India with high-speed internet,” said the space internet company.
Musk replied to Reliance on X, saying “Much appreciated”.
In a statement on Friday, Reliance Industries said, “we welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink.”
“Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land,” said REL in its statement.
“In light of recent remarks about Reliance and the Indian market, we wish to place the facts on record. Like every Indian enterprise, Reliance has grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international, that improve the lives of the people,” the company added.
It further stated “that openness rests on the rule of law. As the Government of India has stated, it applies the same process to every applicant, Indian or foreign. Jio’s own satellite services await clearances”.
At Reliance, “we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best. Jio itself entered India’s crowded telecom market in 2016 as the newest player, with not a single customer”, the company noted.
In just 10 years, Jio has earned the trust of over 530 million customers and given Indians some of the best digital infrastructure and most affordable data in the world.
Starlink has secured a licence to provide satellite communication services in India, but the company still requires security-related clearances and other approvals before it can commercially launch its service.
Last week, Musk took a swipe at billionaire Mukesh Ambani over Starlink’s entry into India, calling him “Dear Prime Minister Ambani,” and accusing him of seeking to maintain a monopoly and questioning whether he would allow the satellite internet service to compete in the country.
In a post on X, Musk addressed Ambani as the “real boss of India” and apologised for not recognising his influence.
“Dear Prime Minister Ambani, Please accept my humble apologies for not realizing that you are the real boss of India,” Musk posted. “Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?” he added.
(IANS)

morning.title: India’s services trade cushion faces a new test
Should India Future-Proof the FRCV With 130mm?
morning.text:
India’s Future Ready Combat Vehicle (FRCV) is being designed for a battlefield that could be far more different from today’s battlefield than the FVCKs were from their predecessors. This raises an obvious question about the main armament: should the Indian Army settle for a conventional 120/125mm gun, or should the new tank be designed from the ground up to accommodate a 130mm-class weapon?
The FRCV’s published requirements currently call for a minimum 120mm main armament, while not a maximum. The vehicle is expected to weigh around 55 tonnes ±5 percent and employ a minimum 1,500-hp powerpack, carry missiles and loitering munition. The attraction of a larger calibre is straightforward: more propellant and a larger projectile offer more scope for kinetic-energy performance.
Rheinmetall’s 130mm Future Gun System, developed for the KF51 Panther, is claimed by the company to be more than 50 percent effective over contemporary 120mm systems, with substantially longer engagement ranges. The system employs an automatic ammunition-handling system and can carry 20 ready rounds in the autoloader. The KF51 experience also shows something interesting: a larger gun is not just a matter of putting a bigger barrel on your tank.
Rheinmetall’s Panther architecture employs an autoloader and a turret designed for the larger weapon. Interestingly, the company’s Hungarian Panther KF51 EVO is initially being developed with a 120mm gun, while its turret architecture allows the subsequent installation of the 130mm weapon. Larger weapon means larger ammunition, ammunition-volume requirements, recoil-management demands and potentially a heavier turret. The changes can impact the vehicle’s centre of gravity, suspension, automotive performance and internal layout.
The FRCV’s 55-tonne requirement existed for a reason. Its specifications explicitly demand transportability by India’s existing rail, road, air and sea infrastructure. The historical Chinese experiments with very large-calibre tank guns also shows that going beyond established calibres creates substantial engineering challenges. China’s Type 98/99 family was experimentally fitted with a 140mm smoothbore, but available historical assessments suggest that such weapons remained experimental rather than becoming standard armament. For India, 140mm should probably be treated as a technology demonstrator calibre rather than an FRCV requirement.
The ammunition burden, autoloader size, recoil and vehicle integration would become increasingly difficult within a 55-tonne envelope.
A 130mm-class weapon is considerably more interesting, since there is already an international development path around it. Rheinmetall has demonstrated a 130mm system, while its Panther architecture shows that a tank can be designed for 120mm initially with potential for 130mm growth. The more significant decision could be whether the FRCV’s turret, ammunition handling system and hull interfaces are designed for calibre growth.
A mature 120/125mm weapon with advanced APFSDS, programmable ammunition, gun-launched missiles and networked targeting could offer the initial capability. At the same time, the turret could incorporate structural and volumetric growth provisions for a future 130mm-class gun.
This would eliminate betting the entire FRCV programme on an immature large-calibre weapon, while avoiding the opposite error: designing a tank in the 2020s whose turret architecture makes a major armament upgrade prohibitively difficult in the 2040s.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

Oh no, what happened to my OOHPod? Windows command prompt puts in a surprise appearance
morning.text: The Windows command line is a marvelous thing, beloved by administrators, but not quite so welcome when you're trying to get a parcel out of a locker. Today's example of Windows behaving badly comes from Ireland and one of the nation's OOHPod postal lockers. An eagle-eyed Register reader, trying to retrieve a parcel, found the locker screen instead teasing a command prompt. For the uninitiated, OOHPod is a service where people retrieve and deposit goods in lockers. Scan your ID (or enter it on a touch screen) and the appropriate locker door springs open and the item (or items) can be retrieved. This all works, assuming whatever is running behind the scenes isn't having a bit of a moment, as our reader experienced. Instead of a welcoming display on the locker's screen, our reader found a blank screen and what looked suspiciously like a minimized command-line window. "I tapped to maximize the window," they told us, "and a sudden command prompt appeared immediately afterward." A command prompt? More like an open invitation for mischief for the average Register reader. After all, while ordinary customers might have been flustered, this was surely an opportunity to teach the engineers who allowed it a lesson. Perhaps a cheeky FORMAT, or possibly the creation of a truly cursed batch file? Or something worse? This is surely what the comment section is made for. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your perspective), no pop-up keyboard appeared for our reader to unleash havoc (not that they would dream of such a thing), and there was no handy socket to plug in a peripheral. The touchscreen accepted another finger jab, and the command window went away, replaced by the usual OOHPod interface, allowing packages to be collected as normal. It was the responsible thing to do, and the bank of lockers was left in a state where the next customer would not have to worry about what this odd cmd.exe thing was all about. However, the question remains. Would you have been so responsible? Or, if there was some way to enter commands, would you have tried to turn a minor bork into a life lesson for the engineer who let Windows give passersby a glimpse of its undercrackers? ®
